extracted.intended_audience: faculty, instructional designers, and course development teams working in higher-education online learning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for designing, developing, and delivering high-quality online courses in higher education, including required documents, pedagogical standards, team roles, technical and administrative practices. Emphasizes pedagogy, support for faculty, and production workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design learning objects to be shareable/reusable/repurposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning objects are designed to be shareable, reusable, and repurposed so that they can work in multiple contexts (McGreal & Elliott).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create modular components that can be adapted across courses and contexts; consider metadata, granularity, and interoperability when authoring learning objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an LMS to organize and standardize course content
rubrics_metrics.description: The first-generation, learning-object-based online course is often delivered through a learning management system (LMS), a software application suite that organizes and standardizes learning content, dividing the course into modules and lessons, supported with quizzes, tests and discussions (Downes, 2005).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure course is structured in modules/lessons with clear navigation; exploit LMS features for assessments, discussions, assignments and secure submission ('drop boxes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit multiple communication and media tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Most LMSs afford developers the use of text; email; asynchronous discussion boards; synchronous utilities such as VoIP; instant-messaging chat features; desktop and application sharing; on-demand video clips and demonstrative animations; interactive activities, simulations, and games; self-grading exercises, quizzes, and examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select technologies that meaningfully support instructional goals (see 'Focus on Sound Pedagogy'); avoid adding tools solely for novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide essential administrative and orientation documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses should contain administrative documents to help instructors organize, prepare, and orient students, especially if they are new to online learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a personalized welcome letter, general info about online learning and tech requirements, access/navigation instructions, student log-in/password info, rules/procedures for interactive tools, a publicly browsable course syllabus (with overview, schedule, required texts, prerequisites, expectations, assignments/deadlines, contact info, support information), and administrative regulations (plagiarism, privacy, appeals, library and counselling access).

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty buy-in and institutional encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators should encourage and support faculty acceptance of online teaching and reassure faculty about their roles relative to technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide encouragement, technical and pedagogical support, training, and ensure that efforts to develop and teach online are recognized in merit, promotion, and tenure processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the same educational standards online as classroom
rubrics_metrics.description: The same educational standards must apply to the development of instruction for the Internet as to any other delivery medium, such as the classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure online instruction against explicitly stated institutional criteria and accepted good-practice frameworks rather than allowing medium to lower standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage contacts between students and faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practice in undergraduate education encourages contacts between students and faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities and communications channels that promote sustained instructor-student interaction to support learning and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop reciprocity and cooperation among students
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practice develops reciprocity and cooperation among students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include structured collaborative activities, peer review, and group tasks to foster student-student interaction and mutual learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active learning techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practice uses active learning techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks requiring learners to do, apply, analyze, or create rather than passively consume content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give prompt feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practice gives prompt feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely, actionable feedback on assignments and participation; exploit technology for quick responses where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize time on task
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practice emphasizes time on task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make workload expectations explicit; design activities to maintain student engagement and scaffold pacing across the semester.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate high expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practice communicates high expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set and articulate clear, challenging learning outcomes and performance standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect diverse talents and ways of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practice respects diverse talents and ways of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple pathways and varied assessment methods to accommodate different learning preferences and backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide timely and appropriate interaction (WICHE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs provide for timely and appropriate interaction between students and faculty, and among students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure course design includes synchronous/asynchronous mechanisms and response-time expectations that support meaningful interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty responsibility and oversight (WICHE)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution’s faculty assumes responsibility for and exercises oversight over distance education, ensuring both the rigour of programs and the quality of instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain faculty governance over curriculum, assessment, and academic standards for online programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide appropriate faculty support services (WICHE)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution provides appropriate faculty support services specifically related to distance education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer instructional design, media production, technical help, and administrative assistance tailored to online teaching needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide appropriate training for online faculty (WICHE)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution provides appropriate training for faculty who teach in distance education programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require and fund training that covers pedagogy, technology, course management, and student engagement strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure student access to library resources (WICHE)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution ensures that students have access to and can effectively use appropriate library resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide remote access, instruction in information literacy, and support for research needs of distance learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate range of student services (WICHE)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution provides adequate access to the range of student services appropriate to support the programs, including admissions, financial aid, academic advising, delivery of course materials, and placement and counselling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend key student services to online learners with clear access points and response procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop tolerance for ambiguity (Fox & Helford)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop tolerance for ambiguity (recognize that there may be no 'right' answer to a given question, and emphasize cognitive flexibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design open-ended problems and discussions that promote critical thinking and multiple perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scaffolding principles (Fox & Helford)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use scaffolding principles (create material that is slightly too difficult for the student, to encourage cognitive 'stretch').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence tasks to progressively build learner competence and provide supports that fade as mastery grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use problems requiring understanding and manipulation of content (Fox & Helford)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use problems that require students to understand and manipulate course content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor problem-based learning, case studies, and applied tasks over rote recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create opportunities for high levels of interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Create opportunities for high levels of interaction, both student-student and instructor-student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design forums, group projects, peer feedback, and instructor-led discussions to sustain meaningful engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate formative assessment throughout the course
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate formative assessment throughout the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frequent low-stakes assessments to monitor learning, provide feedback, and guide instructional adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty should undergo training and experience online learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty should undergo some training before beginning to teach online; one recommended strategy is that faculty initially enroll in an online course themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require or encourage faculty to experience online learning to appreciate student challenges (bandwidth, tools, time-on-task) and to learn new pedagogical/technical skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical proficiencies for online teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical proficiencies include thinking of the online environment as a different kind of classroom; examining other online courses; investing time and effort; weighing importance vs time; being creative and gaining a basic understanding of how technology works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should adapt face-to-face practices where appropriate, learn new online facilitation strategies, and plan creatively to exploit technologies while considering the time cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative skills: ground rules and syllabus enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching online often requires more anticipatory effort; lay out ground rules right away, create a course syllabus that includes class rules, make sure students read it, then stick to those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations clearly at course start, publish rules and deadlines, and consistently enforce them to manage student interactions and workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and use institutional support resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Find out where help is (computing help-desk, media development) and know when to use it; do not wait until you first discover you need them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify contacts for technical, media, and pedagogical help before course launch and incorporate them into the development/teaching workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical baseline skills required for online teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether you possess basic PC skills (familiarity with file structure, opening/copying/saving/moving files, backups, keyboard/mouse, windows, web browsers); be comfortable with email; understand bandwidth and browser differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure instructors have or obtain minimum technical competence; test course content on low-bandwidth and varied browser setups to match student environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and resource management for instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should expect to spend time responding to emails, marking assignments, and managing interactive components; student interaction may be sporadic and surge at times (e.g., course start, technical problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategies such as hiring/assigning technical or TA help for email, creating FAQs, requiring forum-first questions, and directing tech issues to help-desk to manage workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and design course completely before opening
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to plan and design your course completely before it is opened to students; developing materials while teaching can be overwhelming and many underestimate required time and assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest sufficient lead time for development, pilot materials, and finalize design before course launch to create positive first impressions and manageable delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward faculty for innovative online teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should develop processes that encourage and inspire faculty to be creative in a web-based environment and recognize their efforts with tangible benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include online teaching and course development achievements in promotion, tenure, and merit award processes to incentivize quality course design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize an online development unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralizing web development roles into one departmental unit has proved beneficial to ensure that courses are of high quality and meet institutional guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize a unit (para-academics) that liaises with SMEs, manages copyright/permissions, and handles production tasks (project manager, copy editor, IT, coder, media developer, instructional designer, graphic designer, administrative assistant, copyright officer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and curate repositories of reusable learning objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop repositories where educators can submit, use, or exchange learning objects (e.g., Merlot, EDNA, SMETE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributor metadata, interoperability standards, and balance specificity vs generality; be aware of interoperability limitations that may restrict reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage Web 2.0/social tools for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Web 2.0 refers to social networking and virtual communities (blogs, wikis, podcasts, RSS, multi-user domains). The potential benefits for education include opportunities for social networking and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blogs, wikis and social software to facilitate learner-to-learner interaction and shared resource development when pedagogically appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble a multidisciplinary development team
rubrics_metrics.description: Core team might comprise SME/author, graphic designer, web developer, programmer, and instructional designer; larger organizations may subdivide roles, smaller ones may use hyphenated roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure appropriate expertise is available; avoid overloading single individuals with too many unfamiliar tasks; balance creative control with realistic workload and skill fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject Matter Expert (SME) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: SMEs ensure content is an appropriate alternative to lecture content, write exercises/activities/examinations, identify/create textbooks and resources, ensure pedagogical match among objectives, content and assessments, identify materials needing copyright clearance, and provide legible written material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require SMEs to commit through the development cycle, collaborate with designers, and produce clear, accessible source materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional Designer process and tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional design processes: Analysis (define what is to be learned), Design (specify how learning will occur), Development (author and produce materials), Implementation (install the instruction in the real world), Evaluation (determine the impact of instruction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional designers also help SMEs choose pedagogical strategies, create/adapt resources, write and sequence learning outcomes and activities, evaluate instruction, arrange production services, act as project manager and editor, and often act as web developer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web developer responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Web developers should show faculty examples of online materials, describe production using a consistent template (objectives, outline, assignments, evaluation, resources, links, requirements, FAQs), help SMEs/instructors use authoring tools, make course interactive, work with graphic designers, and create design storyboards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide demonstrations to build faculty confidence; ensure consistent templates for student familiarity; in small teams, web developer may perform multiple roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic designer responsibilities and visual continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual design is driven by student and academic needs and course content; graphic designers create templates, navigational icons, visuals to aid recognition and enhance textual content, and ensure continuity for course updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and student usability; design consistent graphical elements aligned with institutional templates to reduce cognitive load for students learning online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programmer and multimedia author responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmers are responsible for program functionality, enabling interactivity using code-based languages or GUI authoring tools; they should help team members understand tool classes and capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose code-based or GUI tools based on project needs (open-source/code for flexibility; GUI for less technical overhead but possible proprietary lock-in). Provide guidance on languages and tools appropriate for desired interactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be deliberate about tool selection and maintainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial GUI software can be expensive and frequently updated, potentially rendering earlier versions obsolete; code-based (often open-source) tools encourage collaborative development and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider long-term maintenance, licensing costs, and interoperability when selecting authoring and development tools.
